title: Open Problem (better query complexity bounds for property testing)
statement_text: It remains a major open problem if better bounds on the query complexity hold for the various general property testing results (which show that natural properties of combinatorial objects can be tested with query complexity depending only on $\epsilon$ and the property, but with enormous or no explicit bounds).
context_text: In property testing one wants to distinguish quickly (with few queries to the object) objects satisfying a property $P$ from objects that are $\epsilon$-far from satisfying it. $P$ is one-sided testable if there are $q(\epsilon)$ and a randomized algorithm making $q(\epsilon)$ queries that always accepts inputs with $P$ and rejects with probability at least $2/3$ inputs that are $\epsilon$-far from $P$; it is two-sided testable if it answers correctly in both cases with probability at least $2/3$. General results give constant (size-independent) query complexity, but with huge bounds: for instance, Alon and Shapira's theorem that every hereditary graph property is one-sided testable gives a bound at least of wowzer type in $1/\epsilon$ (one level above the tower function in the Ackermann hierarchy), because it uses the strong regularity lemma; other results use compactness and give no bound at all, and testing $\sigma$-freeness of permutations with respect to Kendall's tau distance (Klimošová and Kráľ) gives an Ackermann-type bound. For permutations, the rectangular (cut) distance between $\pi_1,\pi_2$ of length $n$ is $\frac1n\max_{S,T}\big||\pi_1(S)\cap T|-|\pi_2(S)\cap T|\big|$ over intervals $S,T\subseteq[n]$, and a permutation property is hereditary if closed under taking subpermutations (patterns). The paper makes progress on this problem for permutations: there is a universal polynomial-in-$1/\epsilon$ query complexity bound (not depending on the property) for two-sided testing of hereditary properties of sufficiently large permutations with respect to the rectangular distance, and a nearly linear bound for a related metric depending on the smallest forbidden subpermutation. This is a general community-level problem rather than a precise conjecture.
